# Kururin Squash!

**Kururin Squash!** is a 2004 puzzle video game developed by Eighting and published by Nintendo for the GameCube. The game was released exclusively in Japan on October 14, 2004 . It is the third and final entry in the Kururin series, following Kuru Kuru Kururin (2001) and Kururin Paradise (2002), and the first game in the series to be released on a home console and to use 3D polygonal graphics ).

## Gameplay

Kururin Squash! maintains the core gameplay concept from the previous Kururin games, where players control a constantly rotating helicopter-like stick called a Helirin (or Heririn) through narrow mazes . The objective is to navigate through these mazes without hitting obstacles or the course sides, as three hits will cause the Helirin to shatter .

The game introduces several new gameplay elements that distinguish it from its predecessors. Players can now pilot specialized helicopters with unique abilities :

* **Punch Heririn**: Can destroy obstacles and enemies but produces recoil, requiring careful timing and positioning

* **Dive Heririn**: Enables underwater navigation, allowing players to submerge and surface through water levels

* **Flame Heririn**: Shoots fire left and right from the wings, used for destroying enemies and solving puzzles

* **Tornado Heririn**: Creates spinning tornadoes for both offensive and defensive purposes

* **Action Helirins**: Five varieties that shoot rapid-fire projectiles

The game also introduces a currency system where gold coins are scattered throughout stages. Collecting all coins in a stage without taking damage earns a perfect clear . Coins can be used in shops to purchase items such as world maps, a Game Boy Advance to GameCube link-up minigame, additional Helirins, customizable HUDs, and instructional movies .

Kururin Squash! features both single-player and multiplayer modes. The multiplayer component includes four-player split-screen gameplay with two modes: Race Mode, where players compete to complete mazes within a target time, and Battle Mode, where players collect coins while using weapons to hinder opponents .

## Plot

The game follows the Kururin family after they win the lottery and embark on a trip around the world . Upon their return journey, they discover that only three family members have returned: Kururin, Kakarin, and Totorin . The player's goal is to find all the missing family members across the game's various levels.

The game's story is presented through cutscenes featuring the characters, though the high-pitched bird voices used for character dialogue have been noted as a minor annoyance in reviews .

## Development

Kururin Squash! was developed by Eighting, who transitioned the series from 2D to 3D computer graphics for this installment . The directors and producers from Kururin Paradise returned to work on this game, which was intended as the final entry in the series .

The game's development team included 31 credited people . Key personnel included:

* **Yasunari Watanabe**: Main Programmer

* **Yuuichi Ochiai**: Program Director

* **Mitsuakira Tatsuta**: Graphics Director

* **Atsuhiro Motoyama**: Composer 

* **Yoichi Kotabe**: Character Designer

The game's visual style received particular praise, with reviewers noting the high-quality 3D graphics, transparency effects, lighting, and particle effects . The levels feature fully polygonal environments with detailed textures and effects, including forests with butterflies visible through transparent floors and various lighting effects .

## Reception

Kururin Squash! received generally positive reviews from critics, with an average score of 75% based on 7 professional reviews . Individual review scores ranged from 60% to 95%, indicating a mixed but overall favorable reception .

### Review scores

| Publication | Score |
| ------------------------------------------- | ----- |
| Planet GameCube | 95% |
| Nintendojo | 90% |
| Nintendo Difference | 75% |
| Retroage | 73% |
| [Eurogamer.net](https://Eurogamer.net) (UK) | 70% |
| Bordersdown | 60% |
| Games TM | 60% |

### Notable reviews

Nintendo World Report gave the game a 9.5/10 rating, praising its brilliant art style, excellent controls, and the new Heririns that "make for some brilliant new puzzles" . The review specifically highlighted the game's graphics, stating: "The levels themselves are fully polygonal, which is a massive leap from the 2D (but still excellent) sprite graphics of the previous games" .

The review also noted the game's sound quality, though it mentioned that the music tracks are relatively short (about a minute before looping) and that the high-pitched bird voices used for character dialogue could be annoying .

HonestGamers listed the game with a 9.5 average score based on the Nintendo World Report review .

## Legacy

Kururin Squash! is the final game in the Kururin series . Despite positive reception, none of the Kururin games were released outside of Japan, with the exception of the original Kuru Kuru Kururin which was released in Europe and Australia .

The Kururin series has had representation in Nintendo's Super Smash Bros. series:

* In Super Smash Bros. Melee, there is a Helirin trophy (misromanized as "Heririn")

* In Super Smash Bros. Brawl, Helirin appears as an Assist Trophy and becomes part of the stage that can be jumped on or slid on

* In Super Smash Bros. Ultimate, Helirin and Kururin return as a shared Spirit

The game is noted for its technical achievements in the puzzle genre, particularly its use of advanced graphics and effects for a puzzle game . Reviewers noted that it was unusual to see such high-quality lighting and particle effects in a puzzle game .

**Kururin Squash!**[[Edit](https://nintendo.fandom.com/wiki/Kururin_Squash!?action=edit)][Talk]

_**Kururin Squash!**_ is a [GameCube](https://nintendo.fandom.com/wiki/Nintendo_GameCube "Nintendo GameCube") video game released by [Nintendo](https://nintendo.fandom.com/wiki/Nintendo "Nintendo") and [Eighting](https://nintendo.fandom.com/wiki/Eighting "Eighting") in [2004](https://nintendo.fandom.com/wiki/2004 "2004"). The game is a puzzle title released exclusively in Japan. In the game you control Kururin who is off to save all of his siblings after they went missing on a family trip across the four countries of the in-game world. 
Gameplay[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fnintendo.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FKururin_Squash%21%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D1&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Playing as Kururin, you go inside of a long rectangular ship that is constantly spinning. The ship, called a [Helirin](https://nintendo.fandom.com/wiki/Helirin "Helirin"), travels through maze-like buildings. If any part of the ship hits a wall three times, he'll have to start over. Your goal is to maneuver the ship in a way so that it doesn't hit any walls. Because it is constantly spinning, this will prove to be a challenge, though you can use this to your advantage as well when you are required to get through tight spaces that can only be entered when your ship is facing in a certain direction, though you must get through it fast incase it continues to spin and crash into the walls. There are three different speeds of the Helirin, and thankfully you can alter the speed to your liking.

Legacy[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fnintendo.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FKururin_Squash%21%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D2&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]

*   The Helirin, who also appeared in _Paradise_, is featured as an [Assist Trophy](https://nintendo.fandom.com/wiki/Assist_Trophy "Assist Trophy") in the [Wii](https://nintendo.fandom.com/wiki/Wii "Wii") video game _[Super Smash Bros. Brawl](https://nintendo.fandom.com/wiki/Super\_Smash\_Bros.\_Brawl "Super Smash Bros. Brawl")_.

Description
-----------

After two adventures on the Game Boy Advance, Kururin goes 3D on the GameCube. In Kururin Squash!, you have to direct Kururin in his helicopter-like Heririn spinning stick through narrow mazes, while avoiding obstacles or courses' sides. The gameplay is spiced up with colourful backgrounds, bizarre enemies, weapons, and bounce pads that change the spin direction. When you get hit three times, the Heririn shatters.

The GameCube version introduces water levels with a submarine, guns, boxing gloves, twisters, flame-throwing, and boss battles. In the main puzzle mode, you have to collect loot and in the race mode, you have to finish the mazes within a target time. Multiplayer includes four-player split-screen frenzy and a battle mode where you have to collect coins while using the weapons to hold off your opponents.

**Kuru Kuru Kururin**[[Edit](https://nintendo.fandom.com/wiki/Kuru_Kuru_Kururin?action=edit)][Talk]

_**Kuru Kuru Kururin**_ is a [Game Boy Advance](https://nintendo.fandom.com/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance "Game Boy Advance") video game launched in [2001](https://nintendo.fandom.com/wiki/2001 "2001") by [Eighting](https://nintendo.fandom.com/wiki/Eighting "Eighting") and [Nintendo](https://nintendo.fandom.com/wiki/Nintendo "Nintendo") during the system's launch in Europe and Japan. The game was never released in North America. Addition to that, a Chinese release of this game was planned for the iQue GBA but was cancelled along with other games (including the first game) due to the high piracy of the console.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IQue#Cancelled_Games) It's an unordinary game that Nintendo officially classifies as a puzzle title. The name originates from the Japanese word "kuru kuru", an onomatopoeia in Japan that is meant to replicate the sound of spinning, while the name Kururin is named after a popular carnival game in Japan. 
Gameplay[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fnintendo.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FKuru_Kuru_Kururin%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D1&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

In _Kuru Kuru Kururin_, the player character is a duck. The titular [Kururin](https://nintendo.fandom.com/wiki/Kururin "Kururin") is the aviator of a [Helirin](https://nintendo.fandom.com/wiki/Helirin "Helirin"). The Helirin is an elongated stick like object that is constantly rotating, whereas in previous similar games (such as a Playstation 1 game called _Irritating Stick_ in America) the stick was still. Though the Helirin is constantly in motion, the player has control over where it goes. The goal is to maneuver around walls and objects. In order to do this, you'll have to move your Helirin when it's in a certain position. For example, if you're attempting to go straight down, though the walls are two tight for you to go through if the Helirin was horizontal, the player is able to wait until the ship is straight up and then go down, but must do so quickly as it'll continue to rotate. If any part of the ship touches an object or the wall, then they will lose health. While you aren't allowed to make the Helirin stop, you can change the position and in some cases the speed. To change the direction it rotates, the player must hit certain special objects that will cause your ship to do so automatically. At the beginning of each stage, the character will have three hearts. Hitting a wall will minus the player of one heart, and once all hearts have been depleted, they'll have to start the entire stage over. There are certain areas in each stage that will replenish your hearts.

Legacy[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fnintendo.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FKuru_Kuru_Kururin%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D2&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Two sequels, _[Kururin Paradise](https://nintendo.fandom.com/wiki/Kururin\_Paradise "Kururin Paradise")_ for the Game Boy Advance and _[Kururin Squash!](https://nintendo.fandom.com/wiki/Kururin\_Squash! "Kururin Squash!")_ for the [GameCube](https://nintendo.fandom.com/wiki/Nintendo_GameCube "Nintendo GameCube"), have been made in [2001](https://nintendo.fandom.com/wiki/2001 "2001") and [2002](https://nintendo.fandom.com/wiki/2002 "2002"), respectively. Unfortunately, none of them ever made it to America. Helirins, of which there are many different kinds, have appeared in the [Wii](https://nintendo.fandom.com/wiki/Wii "Wii") video game _[Super Smash Bros. Brawl](https://nintendo.fandom.com/wiki/Super\_Smash\_Bros.\_Brawl "Super Smash Bros. Brawl")_. In it, they appeared as trophies and as [Assist Trophies](https://nintendo.fandom.com/wiki/Assist_Trophy "Assist Trophy"), where they would become an obstacle that is hard to get past, especially if they push the player over the edge. They also appeared in the game's predecessor _[Super Smash Bros. Melee](https://nintendo.fandom.com/wiki/Super\_Smash\_Bros.\_Melee "Super Smash Bros. Melee")_ as a trophy.

The game was later put on the Wii U's Virtual Console service where in 2016 became the first game in the series to be released in North America. It was also one of the launch games for the [Game Boy Advance - Nintendo Switch Online](https://nintendo.fandom.com/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance_-_Nintendo_Switch_Online "Game Boy Advance - Nintendo Switch Online").

4.title: Kururin Squash! Review - Review
4.content:
Kuru Kuru Kururin debuted for both the Japanese and European Game Boy Advance launches. The idea was deceptively simple -- all you have to do was guide a constantly rotating stick through a maze and reach the goal without hitting any obstacles. Doing so makes you lose time and health. Three hits and you have to start again. Kururin Squash is the third game in the series, and as such, it expands on this basic idea of navigating your way through a maze. In addition to the standard helicopter, you're now able to guide specially designed helicopters that allow you to punch, dive, shoot flames and throw tornados.

As mentioned in my [impressions](http://www.planetgamecube.com/impressions.cfm?action=profile&id=716), the first thing that will strike you about the game is the incredible graphic style. (Take a look at the intro, which is available for [download](http://www.planetgamecube.com/news.cfm?action=item&id=5745) to see for yourself.) The graphics are crisp and bright, and all the characters in cutscenes are moved around as though they were puppets on sticks, with additional sticks used for controlling their arms. If they want to change expressions, the character will flip around and a completely different version of the same character will be on the other side. It's a really refreshing look, and I've never seen anything like it before.

The levels themselves are fully polygonal, which is a massive leap from the 2D (but still excellent) sprite graphics of the previous games. The mazes have some great transparency effects that allow you to see, for example, forests with butterflies underneath you. Other high points for the GameCube version are the lighting and particle effects. It's quite strange to see such great effects in a puzzle game, but there they are. Dust will kick up when you punch walls, lasers will leave light halos, and there are surprisingly massive explosions for destroying enemies. Enemies caught in tornados will be spun high in the air and fly right towards the camera. The effects are subtle, but very pretty.

The game's soundtrack is quite decent. Although the music tracks clock in at around a minute before they begin to loop, they're pleasant enough for you not to notice. There're a large variety of instruments used, including a very Seventies-like "wikky-wa" guitar melody when you successfully complete a level. Each level's music suits its area - the sky levels have airy, futuristic music, the ocean level music is wonderfully mellow, and the boss theme is suitably frantic. Most of the sound effects are strikingly similar to the Game Boy Advance games, which is not a problem, as it keeps a sense of familiarity. Most other sounds are similar to typical video-game sounds, but it's wonderfully satisfying to hear the "whoosh" of the flamethrower Heririn (or helicopter). The only problem that I have with the game's sound are the noises used for the character speech. It's a kind of high-pitched tweeting, and because I use headphones a lot, it rattles right through my brain.

Kururin Squash mixes elements from the previous games -- that is, the guiding of a constantly rotating stick through a maze without hitting anything -- and adds new helicopters that cause the player to think a bit more carefully when guiding them. The Punch Heririn can be used to destroy obstacles and enemies, but you get a bit of recoil from it, so you need to allow a little leeway when you use it. The Dive Heririn will cause you to think on two different levels, as you'll have to play through sections of levels which need to be quickly navigated by rising and submerging again, in some cases fighting strong currents and whirlpools. The Flame Heririn makes things incredibly tough, as the levels take place entirely on-rails. Using the Control Stick will freely rotate the Heririn, and you'll occasionally need to dodge precariously placed crystals and massive enemies that chase you throughout the level. The Tornado Heririn also allows for some clever puzzles. Some will see you temporarily blocking an enemy dispenser; others will have you safely riding in a tornado as you launch it down a corridor full of flamethrowers. You'll also need to learn to use those special Heririns for clever boss battles. Eighting have gone all-out in using the GameCube to create an expanded Kururin experience.

Kururin Squash is also the first game in the series to introduce currency. Strewn throughout the stages are gold coins -- collect all of them in a stage in addition to not getting hurt at all and you'll earn yourself a perfect clear. Coins can also be earned by defeating enemies. You won't need to collect those, as they'll be collected automatically. Coins can be used in the various shops on the map screen (the Carnies from Kururin Paradise make cameo appearances in running the shops), where you'll be able to purchase various items. They include world maps, a GBA to GC Link Up Mini-Game, additional Heririns, Customizable HUDs, and Teacher Hare Movies that show you how to beat the stages safely. Some of the Heririns include a Chocolate Bar, a Tank, and a Heririn with Nintendo logo blades that plays the Super Mario Bros. coin sound when you press the horn. Collecting all of the shop items is purely optional, but it makes for a good reason to return to the game.

The Battle Multiplayer in Squash definitely seems to be more fun than the Race Mode. In Race, avid Kururin players have a distinct advantage over novices, whereas with Battle it's all about beating each other up, powering up, and collecting the most coins. The tables can quickly turn if you have the right power up. In Race, although the leader gets a handicap of becoming larger, they can easily overcome this if they're a skilled player. The GBA to GC link-up game is basically just a memory match game, which is a bit of a shame.

The biggest injustice is that this will be the third Kururin game to not see the light of day outside of Japan. It's totally bizarre as to why, as the game represents everything that Nintendo could possibly want -- a simple, yet fun concept, a new franchise, and a game that can be played without having to worry about the language barrier. If you like your puzzle games and have not heard of the Kururin series before, I'd **highly** recommend getting this game. Actually, I'd recommend all three, as they're all stellar games. Kururin Squash continues the series' legacy of great fun, lastability, and typical Japanese wackiness. As an import game, the language barrier is zilch.
